title: How Presidential Debates Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the history of U.S. presidential debates, starting with the 1858 Lincoln-Douglas Senate debates and Lincoln's later refusal to debate in 1860. They cover the 1948 Dewey-Stassen radio debate, the League of Women Voters' 1976 televised debates, and the 1960 Kennedy-Nixon debate that made TV appearance central. They discuss the Equal Time Provision of the 1934 Communications Act, Nixon's veto to keep it, Carter skipping the 1980 debate with Reagan and Anderson, and the 1987 Memorandum of Understanding between the Bush and Dukakis campaigns that pushed the League out. They describe the Commission on Presidential Debates as a bipartisan group that hosts official debates, the 1992 and 1996 Perot exclusions, debate formats and qualification rules, the spin after debates, memorable gaffes (Quayle, Reagan's age question to Mondale's laugh), and social media town halls in 2008. The episode closes with listener mail about a soldier in Afghanistan and a shout-out to his family.

segments.title: Opening banter and GOP primary debates
segments.summary: The hosts chat casually, then discuss the 2011 Republican primary debates, a Saturday Night Live sketch about candidates being sidelined, and the point that these are not official presidential debates.

segments.title: Lincoln-Douglas debates and early radio debate
segments.summary: Lincoln challenged Stephen Douglas to debates during the 1858 Illinois Senate race on slavery, and Lincoln lost. Lincoln did not debate in 1860. The next presidential debate was the 1948 radio debate between Dewey and Stassen.

segments.title: League of Women Voters first televised debate
segments.summary: The League of Women Voters hosted the first televised presidential debate in 1956, featuring candidates from all parties in a free-for-all format.

segments.title: Kennedy-Nixon 1960 Great Debate
segments.summary: The 1960 Kennedy-Nixon debate was the first televised debate between the two major party nominees. Nixon looked pale and ill in a gray suit while Kennedy looked healthy. Radio listeners favored Nixon, TV viewers favored Kennedy, showing the power of appearance on television.

segments.title: Equal Time Provision and Nixon's avoidance of debates
segments.summary: The 1934 Communications Act's Equal Time Provision let candidates avoid debates, since giving one candidate airtime required giving rivals equal time. Nixon used a presidential veto to keep the provision, so he could dodge debates.

segments.title: League of Women Voters era and Carter-Reagan 1980 debate
segments.summary: The League of Women Voters returned to host debates from 1976 to 1984 with an open format allowing follow-up questions. An FCC ruling treated the debates as bona fide news events, exempting them from equal time. Carter refused to debate Reagan and independent John Anderson in 1980, and the debate went on without him.

segments.title: 1987 Memorandum of Understanding and creation of the Commission on Presidential Debates
segments.summary: The Bush and Dukakis campaigns signed a secret Memorandum of Understanding in 1987 that restricted audiences, panelists, and follow-up questions. The League of Women Voters resigned as host, and the two parties created the bipartisan Commission on Presidential Debates to host official debates.

segments.title: Commission's role, Perot exclusion, and debate formats
segments.summary: The Commission plans debates about a year out and acts as a shield for campaigns' unpopular decisions. In 1992 and 1996 Clinton and Dole kept Ross Perot out, and the Commission announced it. The hosts describe moderator, panel, and town hall formats and the qualification rules.
